essays.stem: Describe the main types of kitchen knife and say what each one is used for.
essays.modelAnswer: The cook's or chef's knife, with a blade of about 20–25 cm, is the main all-purpose knife. It is used for chopping, slicing, dicing and mincing vegetables, herbs and meat. The paring knife is small, with a blade of about 7–10 cm, and is used for peeling, trimming and fine work on small fruit and vegetables. The boning knife has a narrow, pointed blade and is used to take bones out of meat and poultry. The filleting knife has a thin, flexible blade for taking fish off the bone and removing the skin. The bread knife has a serrated, saw-like edge for cutting bread, cakes and soft items such as tomatoes without squashing them. The carving knife has a long, narrow blade for slicing cooked meat, such as roast pork or ham. The cleaver is heavy, with a wide blade, for chopping through bones, such as goat for curry goat. The turning knife has a short curved blade for shaping vegetables. Using the right knife for each job is safer and gives a better result.
markingPoints: Cook's knife: the all-purpose knife for chopping, slicing and dicing
Paring knife: peeling and trimming small items
Boning and filleting knives: removing bones from meat; filleting fish
Bread knife (serrated) and carving knife (cooked meat)
Cleaver for bones; right knife for the job is safer

essays.stem: Explain the safety rules for carrying, passing and putting down knives, and for working with them in a busy kitchen.
essays.modelAnswer: I carry a knife with the point down and the edge facing back, held close to my side, and I say 'knife' or 'behind you' when I walk past people. I walk, never run, with a knife. I never carry more than one knife loose in my hand; if I need to move several, I use a knife roll or tray. To pass a knife, I lay it down on the bench and let the other person pick it up, instead of handing it over. When I put a knife down, I lay it flat on the bench or board, away from the edge, with the blade facing in, never hidden under cloths, peelings or food. If a knife falls, I step back and let it fall, and never try to catch it. I keep my eyes on the work while I cut, and I do not talk with my hands while holding a knife. I use knives only for cutting food, never to open tins or as a screwdriver, and I never leave a knife in the sink.
markingPoints: Carry point down, edge back, by your side; warn others; never run
Pass by laying the knife on the bench
Put it down flat, away from the edge, never hidden under food or cloths
Never catch a falling knife; step back
Concentrate; use knives only for cutting food; never leave them in the sink

essays.stem: Describe how to set up a safe and hygienic cutting workstation.
essays.modelAnswer: First I wash my hands and put on a clean uniform, apron and hair cover. I clean and sanitise the bench. I choose the right chopping board for the food, using the Centre's colour code, for example green for salad and fruit or red for raw meat. I put a damp cloth or a non-slip mat under the board so it cannot slip. I place the board near the front of the bench, with enough room to work. I choose the right knife for the job, check it is sharp, clean and in good condition, with a firm handle, and lay it flat on the board with the edge facing away from me. I set out a bowl or tray for the prepared food, a separate bowl for peelings and waste, and a clean cloth. I keep the area clear of things I do not need, and keep the floor dry and free of peelings. I keep raw meat and ready-to-eat food on separate boards and areas. Then I read the recipe so I know the cut and size I need.
markingPoints: Hygiene first: hands washed, clean uniform, bench sanitised
Correct colour-coded board on a damp cloth or non-slip mat
Right, sharp, sound knife placed safely
Bowls for prepared food and waste; uncluttered bench and dry floor
Raw and ready-to-eat kept apart; recipe checked for the cut needed

essays.stem: Describe the claw grip and the bridge grip, and explain why each one is used.
essays.modelAnswer: The claw grip is used to hold food, such as an onion, carrot or cho cho, while slicing or dicing it. I curl the fingers of the hand holding the food, so the fingertips are tucked in and the thumb is behind the fingers. The flat side of the knife rests against the knuckles, which guide the blade. As I cut, I move my clawed hand back slowly so the slices are even. Because the fingertips are tucked away, the blade cannot reach them. The bridge grip is used to cut round or larger items in half, such as a tomato, potato or plantain. I make a bridge over the food with my thumb on one side and my fingers on the other, holding it firmly. I put the knife under the bridge and cut down and through, away from my hand, so the blade never passes under my fingers. Both grips keep the food steady so it does not roll, give neat, even cuts, and keep the fingers away from the blade, which prevents cuts.
markingPoints: Claw: fingertips tucked in, thumb behind, knuckles guide the blade
Claw used for slicing and dicing; hand moves back for even cuts
Bridge: thumb and fingers form a bridge over round items
Bridge used to halve round or large items; blade goes under the bridge, away from the fingers
Both keep the food steady and the fingers away from the blade

essays.stem: Explain how to keep a knife sharp, including honing with a steel and sharpening with a whetstone.
essays.modelAnswer: A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one, because it needs less force and is less likely to slip. To hone with a steel, I hold the steel point down, resting on a damp cloth on the bench. I hold the knife at about 15–20° to the steel, or as the maker advises, and draw the blade down and towards me along the steel, from heel to tip, with light, even pressure. I do the same on the other side, about 5 to 10 times each side. Honing straightens the edge and is done often, even before each task. When honing no longer works, the knife needs sharpening on a whetstone. I soak or wet the stone as its maker says and put it on a damp cloth so it does not move. I hold the knife at the same angle and push the blade across the stone, from heel to tip, several times on each side, using the coarse side first and the fine side to finish. Then I wash and dry the knife and test it carefully on a tomato or paper.
markingPoints: A sharp knife is safer (less force, less slipping)
Honing: steel held steady, knife at about 15–20°, heel to tip, both sides
Honing straightens the edge and is done often
Sharpening on a whetstone (wetted, steadied) at the same angle, coarse then fine
Wash, dry and test the knife safely after

essays.stem: Describe how to dice an onion safely and evenly.
essays.modelAnswer: I set up a board on a damp cloth and use a sharp cook's knife. I cut a thin slice off the top (stalk end) of the onion, but leave the root end on, because it holds the layers together. I cut the onion in half from top to root using the bridge grip, then peel off the papery skin. I lay one half flat side down on the board, so it is steady. Holding it with the claw grip, I make even cuts from near the root towards the top, close together, without cutting through the root. Then I make one or two careful cuts across, parallel to the board, keeping my fingers on top and the blade moving away from my hand. Finally, using the claw grip, I slice down across the first cuts, moving my hand back each time, so the onion falls into small, even dice. I stop before the root end and put the root in the stock bowl. I put the diced onion in a bowl, and wipe the board before the next one.
markingPoints: Safe set-up: steady board and a sharp cook's knife
Leave the root on; halve with the bridge grip; peel
Flat side down; cuts towards the root, not through it
Horizontal cuts with care, then slice across with the claw grip
Even dice; root kept for stock; tidy board

essays.stem: Describe how to cut a carrot into julienne, and then into brunoise.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash and peel the carrot and cut off the ends. I cut it into lengths of about 4–5 cm, or as the recipe says. I cut a thin slice off one side of each piece so it lies flat and does not roll. Then I cut each piece into thin, even slices, about 2–3 mm thick, using the claw grip. I stack a few slices and cut them lengthways into thin strips, also about 2–3 mm wide. These even matchstick strips are the julienne. To make brunoise, I gather a bundle of the julienne strips, lay them side by side and, using the claw grip, cut across them at the same 2–3 mm spacing. This gives tiny, even dice of about 2–3 mm, which is brunoise. I keep the cuts as even as possible, so the pieces cook in the same time and look neat. I put the trimmings in a bowl to use in stock. I check the sizes with a ruler, and put the cuts in a covered, labelled container in the fridge until I use them.
markingPoints: Prepare the carrot: wash, peel, cut into even lengths, square off to stop rolling
Slice evenly about 2–3 mm thick with the claw grip
Cut the slices into strips about 2–3 mm wide to make julienne
Cut across the julienne to make brunoise, tiny dice about 2–3 mm
Even sizes checked; trimmings used for stock; cuts covered, labelled and chilled

essays.stem: Explain what you should do if you or a co-worker is cut by a knife in the kitchen.
essays.modelAnswer: First I stop work and put the knife down safely. For a small cut, I wash my hands, then rinse the cut under clean running water and dry it. I press on it with a clean dressing to stop the bleeding. I cover it with a blue waterproof plaster, which is easy to see if it falls into food, and wear a disposable glove over it if it is on the hand. I throw away any food that blood may have touched, and clean and sanitise the board, knife and bench. For a deep cut, or one that will not stop bleeding, I press firmly on it with a clean pad, raise the hand above the heart if I can, and call the first-aider at once. If the cut is very bad, the person may need a doctor or an ambulance. In every case, I report the cut to the supervisor and it is written in the accident book. The supervisor checks why it happened, for example a blunt knife or a slipping board, so it can be stopped from happening again.
markingPoints: Stop work and put the knife down safely
Small cut: clean, press, blue waterproof plaster, glove over it
Throw away food that blood may have touched; clean and sanitise the area
Deep cut: firm pressure, raise, call the first-aider; medical help if needed
Report and record in the accident book; find the cause to stop it happening again

essays.stem: Describe how to clean, sanitise and store knives and chopping boards after use, and say why each step matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I clean a knife straight after use, so food does not dry on it and germs do not grow or spread to other food. I wash it one at a time in hot water with detergent, holding it by the handle with the edge away from me, and I never leave it in the sink, where someone could put a hand in and be cut. I rinse it, then sanitise it with the Centre's sanitiser or very hot water. I dry it carefully with a clean cloth or paper towel, wiping from the spine towards the edge, or leave it to air dry in a safe rack. I store it in a knife block, on a magnetic rack or in a knife roll with a blade guard, never loose in a drawer, so the edge stays sharp and no one is cut. Chopping boards are scraped, washed in hot water and detergent, rinsed, sanitised and stood on their edges in a rack to air dry, so air reaches both sides. I check boards for deep cuts and cracks, where germs can hide, and report any that need replacing.
markingPoints: Clean straight after use (reason: food dries on, germs spread)
Wash one at a time, edge away; never leave in the sink (reason)
Rinse, sanitise, and dry safely from spine to edge or air dry
Store in a block, rack or roll with guards, never loose (reasons)
Boards washed, sanitised, air dried on edge and checked for damage

essays.stem: Describe how to prepare Jamaican seasoning ingredients (onion, scallion, thyme, garlic and Scotch bonnet pepper) with a knife, safely and hygienically.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash my hands and the produce, set up a clean vegetable board on a damp cloth, and use a sharp cook's knife and a paring knife. For the onion, I peel it and dice it, using the bridge grip to halve it and the claw grip to cut it. For the scallion, I trim the root and any dry tops, then line up the stems and slice them across, using the claw grip, into thin rings. For the thyme, I strip the leaves off the stalk by running my fingers down it, or I keep whole sprigs if the recipe says. For the garlic, I crush each clove with the flat of the knife to loosen the skin, peel it, then slice and chop it finely using a rocking action, keeping the knife point on the board. For the Scotch bonnet pepper, I wear disposable gloves, cut it in half with a paring knife, and scrape out the seeds and white membrane if the recipe wants less heat, then chop it finely. I wash the board and knife after the pepper, take off the gloves and wash my hands, and never touch my eyes.
markingPoints: Hygienic, safe set-up: hands washed, board on a damp cloth, sharp knives, produce washed
Onion and scallion cut with the bridge and claw grips
Thyme leaves stripped; garlic crushed, peeled and finely chopped with a rocking action
Gloves for Scotch bonnet; seeds and membrane removed for less heat
Board and knife washed after the pepper; hands washed; eyes not touched

practical1.title: Classical vegetable cuts: a labelled display tray from each member
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare a display of classical vegetable cuts. Each member sets up their own safe workstation and produces one tray with the following cuts, each about 50 g and in a labelled pile: julienne and brunoise of carrot; jardinière (batons) and macédoine of carrot, cho cho or potato; paysanne of carrot or cho cho; chiffonade of callaloo or lettuce; diced onion; finely chopped garlic and parsley or thyme; and tomato concassé. The assessor gives the sizes on a card (for example julienne about 2–3 mm thick and about 4 cm long). Members measure a sample of each cut with a ruler before laying it out. Together, the group sorts all trimmings into a bowl for stock and the waste into the bin, then washes, sanitises and stores the knives and boards. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every tray is done and the area is clean.
materials: For each member: 2 carrots, 1 cho cho or potato, 1 onion, 2 tomatoes, garlic, a few leaves of callaloo or lettuce, parsley or thyme
Cook's knife and paring knife for each member, and a steel
A chopping board in the Centre's colour for vegetables, and a damp cloth or non-slip mat, for each member
Bowls for prepared food, trimmings and waste
A pan of boiling water and a bowl of iced water for the concassé
A 30 cm ruler and the assessor's size card
Detergent, food-safe sanitiser, clean cloths, knife block or knife rolls
photos: Each member's workstation set up, with the board on a damp cloth
A member using the claw grip, and a member using the bridge grip
The julienne, then the brunoise cut from it, with a ruler beside them
The tomatoes blanched, peeled and deseeded for concassé
Each member's finished, labelled display tray
The knives and boards cleaned and stored, and the area clean
checklist: Set up a steady board, with bowls for food and waste, and a sharp, clean knife
Used the claw and bridge grips correctly, with fingertips kept clear of the blade
Carried, put down and passed knives safely throughout
Cut each item to the size on the card, with even pieces
Made each classical cut correctly and labelled it
Kept waste low, saving clean trimmings for stock
Kept the bench and floor clear of peelings
Washed, sanitised, dried and stored knives and boards correctly
safety: Carry knives point down by your side, and never try to catch a falling knife
Put a damp cloth or non-slip mat under every board
Never leave a knife in the sink or under peelings
Use dry oven cloths and take care with boiling water when blanching tomatoes
Report every cut, however small, and cover it with a blue plaster and a glove

practical2.title: Knife care, a tropical fruit platter and Jamaican green seasoning
practical2.brief: As a group, look after your knives and use them to prepare a fruit platter and a batch of Jamaican green seasoning. First, each member inspects their knives and reports any damage, hones a cook's knife on a steel, and, with the assessor watching, sharpens a knife on a whetstone, then tests it safely on a tomato. Next, each member prepares at least one fruit for a platter for 10: for example, peeling, coring and slicing a pineapple; cutting mango cheeks and scoring them; peeling and seeding a pawpaw; cutting watermelon wedges; and cutting orange segments. The group arranges the platter, covers it and puts it in the fridge. Then the group makes green seasoning: each member prepares at least one of onion, scallion, thyme, garlic and Scotch bonnet pepper (with gloves), and the group blends them. Finally, every member cleans, sanitises and stores their knives and board. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the platter and seasoning are done and the area is clean.

Pineapple, mangoes, pawpaw, watermelon, oranges, limes
Onion, scallion, thyme, garlic, Scotch bonnet peppers, vinegar or lime juice, salt

Boards in the Centre's colour code, damp cloths, bowls
Platter, cling film, labelled containers, disposable gloves
Detergent, food-safe sanitiser, clean cloths, knife block or knife rolls
photos: Each member honing a knife on the steel
A member sharpening on the whetstone, and the tomato test
The pineapple standing flat with the top and base cut off, then the skin removed

checklist: Checked the knives for damage and reported any problem
Honed with the steel held steady and the knife at a suitable angle
Sharpened on the whetstone safely and tested the edge without touching it
Used the right knife and grip for each fruit, cutting away from the body
Cut neat, even pieces with little waste, and arranged them well

safety: Steady the steel and the whetstone on a damp cloth; never hone towards your hand
Test sharpness on food or paper, never on your finger
Stand a pineapple or melon on a flat cut end before cutting down
Fit the blender lid and guard before switching on, and unplug it before cleaning
